editorial.headline: Beach Tourism: Open Nationally, Blocked for PMA in Bali
editorial.standfirst: Beach-centred visitor facilities may be fully foreign-owned nationally, but Bali’s permanent risk-based moratorium prevents PMA registration at the recorded Large-scale risk assessment.
editorial.body:
A foreign investor cannot register a beach-tourism activity under this code in Bali today, even though national policy opens it to PMA with foreign ownership up to 100 per cent. That contrast is the central fact of the record. At the Large scale, every stated scope is rated Low or Medium-Low risk in OSS, and the provincial moratorium blocks PMA registration for both risk classes. National foreign openness and Bali PMA registrability are separate results here: Bali’s outcome is a registration block, not a reduction of the national ownership ceiling.

In practical terms, this activity provides a place and facilities for enjoying natural beauty where the beach is the principal attraction. The beach is not incidental scenery; it is the core setting around which the visitor offer is organised. The scope expressly includes the rental of facilities such as bathrooms, lockers and seating. Food and drink services and accommodation may also be provided. Those additions can sit alongside the principal beach-based activity, but they do not displace the beach as the stated centre of the business.

The activity is open at Micro, Small, Medium and Large scales. The record names all four classifications without attaching a different PMA percentage to any of them. Nationally, its PMA status is TERBUKA, with a maximum foreign holding of 100 per cent under Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. This means full foreign ownership is permitted nationally for the activity. The breadth of the listed scales answers who may register it in the national framework; it does not alter the stated foreign-ownership ceiling.

Bali requires a separate reading. Its recorded status is BLOCCATO_CLASSE_RISCHIO because the provincial rule blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA, island-wide and permanently. The Bali reason identifies the Large-scale OSS assessment across every scope as Low or Medium-Low and notes the moratorium of 13 May 2026. The rule is recorded as originating in Gubernur letter B.27.000/642/PM/DPMPTSP. There is no Bali-specific ownership percentage or partnership condition in the record to soften or replace the national figure. For a foreign-owned registration in Bali, the operative answer is block, notwithstanding the 100 per cent national ceiling.
editorial.pullQuote: A 100 per cent national foreign-ownership ceiling does not overcome Bali’s permanent PMA registration block.
